items.title: Government to cut EDMO qualifying period to six months
items.summary: As reported by Local Government Lawyer, the government plans to cut the qualifying period for Empty Dwelling Management Orders from two years to six months. EDMOs let a council manage a long-term empty property for up to seven years while the owner keeps title. The reforms ease evidential requirements, making an EDMO simpler to secure via the Residential Property Tribunal.

items.title: Shared owners who fled London fire still liable for rent and service charges
items.summary: As reported by Inside Housing, shared owners who fled their London block after a fatal fire on 12 September still face rent and service charges for at least a month while their homes are inaccessible. Landlord Notting Hill Genesis said residents must keep paying under their agreements. One shared owner said she faces about 650 pounds a month in service charges plus around 900 pounds in rent.

items.title: Allocation to track when enforcing disrepair settlements
items.summary: As reported by Local Government Lawyer, the Designated Civil Judge on appeal in S v HA held that CPR rule 26.9(1)(b) still applies when a tenant enforces a compromise over outstanding disrepair works, even though framed as breach of contract. The small claims track is not automatic where the tenant seeks repairs and damages above 1,000 pounds. Allocation matters in settled disrepair claims.

items.title: Use costs to clamp down on 'AI slop', urges former lord chancellor
items.summary: As reported by the Law Society Gazette, former lord chancellor Sir Robert Buckland KC has suggested judges use the costs regime to deter litigants in person from flooding courts with AI-generated material. He said AI has removed the natural brake on prolixity, since generating documents costs the filer almost nothing, and that AI-generated conduct should still count as conduct under the costs rules. He stressed that uninformed use should be treated differently from irresponsible use.

items.title: Law centres axe service as funding squeeze tightens
items.summary: As reported by the Law Society Gazette, South West London Law Centres has disbanded its employment team and warned its housing team is at risk amid a staff exodus and cuts to external funding. The group is increasingly reliant on grant funding because of legal aid cuts and loss of funding from the Equalities and Human Rights Commission and local authorities. It has urged the government to keep the Access to Justice Foundation as the sole recipient of unclaimed class action cash.

items.title: Poor records weaken landlords' mould defence, barrister says
items.summary: As reported by Property118, property barrister Jeffrey Zitron of The Barrister Group Chambers says landlords lose most damp and mould disputes through how they handle complaints rather than the law itself. Those who cannot show when a property was last inspected are worse placed to contest a tenant's claim. Damp and mould drives most of the chambers' disrepair work.

items.title: Regulator finds life critical fire safety defects in 12 per cent of social housing blocks in England
items.summary: As reported by Housing Today, the Regulator of Social Housing's Q1 2026/27 survey found a life critical fire safety defect in external wall systems in 12.1 per cent of relevant buildings over 11 metres in England, up from 11.6 per cent, some 2,078 of 17,258 blocks. Around 76.7 per cent should be remediated within five years. The regulator warned that risks must be managed promptly.

items.title: Onward Homes brings damp and mould services in-house to meet Awaab's Law demand
items.summary: As reported by Housing Today, Manchester-based Onward Homes said it has seen more damp and mould cases since Awaab's Law was introduced, despite repair demand falling 2.8 per cent year on year. The 35,000-home provider has taken damp and mould services in-house, along with gas servicing, to cut reliance on contractors. Landlords are restructuring to meet new damp and mould repair timescales.

items.title: Legal aid providers still absorb 10p gap as Legal Aid Agency holds mileage rate at 45p
items.summary: As reported by the Law Society Gazette, HM Treasury raised the approved mileage allowance to 55p a mile, but the Legal Aid Agency has not adapted, so firms still recover only 45p. The Law Society and Legal Aid Practitioners Group say each journey must now be recorded twice, adding unremunerated work. They warn the gap deepens the legal aid recruitment crisis behind much housing disrepair work.

items.title: Upper Tribunal confirms service charge liability follows the lease in mixed-tenure developments
items.summary: As reported by Local Government Lawyer, the Upper Tribunal upheld a decision in Notting Hill Home Ownership Ltd v Samoail that service charge recovery depends on the lease terms, not the costs a landlord incurs under a superior lease. The landlord could not recover estate charges for facilities its shared ownership leaseholders could not use, and failed to vary the leases.

items.title: Scottish regulator reports more than 40,000 damp and mould cases resolved ahead of Awaab's Law
items.summary: As reported by Housing Today, the Scottish Housing Regulator's first review of its damp and mould performance indicators found social landlords resolved more than 40,000 cases in 2025-26, taking an average of 26 days, with no recurrence in 92 per cent of them. Condensation was the most common cause of reopened cases at 52 per cent. Awaab's Law takes effect in Scotland on 6 October 2026.

items.title: Updated HHSRS brings fewer hazard categories and a simplified scoring system
items.summary: As reported by the National Residential Landlords Association, the updated Housing Health and Safety Rating System came into force on 23 June 2026 and applies to any inspection started on or after 22 June 2026. Prescribed hazard descriptions fall from 29 to 21, and the former A to J bands are replaced by High, Medium and Low scores, where 1,000 or above counts as High.
